verdict: OK to lend in Bhagalpur silk weaving, but only to yarn-secured, flood-safe weavers and traders with verified order books; avoid wage-piece weavers and low-lying Champanagar units until the cocoon bank and yarn supply are proven.
title: Bhagalpur silk weaving & sarees: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Bhagalpur silk is a power-loom and handloom weaving trade that converts bought-in silk yarn into sarees and fabric, and the district does not produce its own yarn.** Weavers depend on intermediaries for reshami thread, and those intermediaries charge heavily when yarn is scarce [2]. Most weavers work on others' orders for piece wages of about Rs 300-400 a day, so they are labour, not borrowers [3]. The real lending units are the trader-mahajans who hold the order book and the few weavers who own looms and buy yarn. ## Where cash and value sit
**Value sits in the finished saree and the order, not in the loom.** Working capital is inventory-led: yarn must be bought ahead, fabric takes time on the power loom, and receivables follow festive and wedding orders [9]. The sector is fixed- and working-capital intensive, so funding needs are high [8]. Pricing power is weak because weavers do not get the right price for cloth [2]. So when a proposal lands, check who holds the yarn stock and who carries the unsold saree; if the borrower is only a wage weaver, ask why he needs a loan at all. The structural break is yarn: no local spinning means middlemen set the price [2]. The district administration is setting up a cocoon bank and discussing stalls so weavers can sell directly [2]; that source carries a 2024 update date, so treat it as old. Local coverage is thin on borrower-level numbers, so lean on first principles and peers. ## Where to grow
**Bihar's electricity demand is running 14.1% Apr-to-date against India's 9.5%, a real local tailwind for power-loom capacity [D].** Pursue loom-owning weavers and trader-mahajans with confirmed festive and wedding orders, and units in high-ground locations. Avoid wage-piece weavers, Champanagar low-lying sheds, and anyone whose yarn comes only from a single middleman. Peer Sai Silks held gross margins at 42% in Q1 FY2027 even with flat revenue [4], and Siyaram saw demand spike only around key events [7] — so underwrite occasion demand, not steady demand. ## How to grow safely
**Structure against yarn and flood, not against hope.** Take hypothecation of yarn and finished stock, and a charge on the loom. Keep tenor short and matched to the order cycle. Take every month: stock statement, order register, yarn purchase bills, and loom-running days. Ask for flood-level photos of the unit. ICRA notes that low leverage and longer-tenor term debt improve coverage in downturns [10], so size term loans to the borrower's cash flow, not to the loom's price. ## Early-warning signs
- **Order cancellations or delayed delivery** (monthly): two cancellations in a quarter -> freeze fresh limits and inspect stock. - **Yarn price paid to middlemen** (monthly): a sharp rise without a matching saree price -> shift to cash-margin lending. - **Loom idle days** (weekly in monsoon): water in the shed -> stop disbursal and move the borrower to a safer site. - **Stock ageing** (monthly): unsold sarees past one festive season -> demand stock auction before renewing. - **Electricity connection status** (quarterly): disconnection -> treat as a stress signal and recall.
